title: You Trust Butterflies in Your Stomach, Yet a Scary Bridge Fakes Falling in Love
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Dutton & Aron (1974): The 230-Foot Swaying Capilano Canyon Bridge — Mistaking Fear Adrenaline for Romantic Spark!, grounded in Donald G. Dutton, Arthur P. Aron (1974) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that in *1974 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology), UBC psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron found nature's ultimate adrenaline laboratory in North Vancouver: the Capilano Canyon Suspension Bridge — a 5-foot-wide, 450-foot-long plank bridge that tilts, sways, and wobbles between low wire handrails 230 feet above churning rapids and jagged canyon boulders*.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how amygdala, insula, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that just upstream spanned the perfect Low-Fear Control Bridge: a heavy, solid, non-swaying cedar-wood bridge sitting a calm 10 feet above a shallow, quiet stream.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Donald G. Dutton, Arthur P. Aron (1974). Some evidence for heightened sexual attraction under conditions of high anxiety. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037031
- Shirley A. Feldman-Summers (1974). Blunders and interpersonal attraction under conditions of dependency. Journal of Abnormal Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0036692
- Craig A. Foster, Betty S. Witcher, W. Keith Campbell, Jeffrey D. Green (1998). Arousal and attraction: Evidence for automatic and controlled processes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037//0022-3514.74.1.86

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
